title: Fizz Buzz
description: Brute force to optimized: composable divisibility checks and a modulo-free counter approach.

blocks.text: 1. Problem Statement
Problem Summary: FizzBuzz is a counting exercise with a twist. Instead of always printing the number, certain numbers get replaced by a word, based on what they are divisible by.

blocks.caption: What goes in, what comes out

blocks.text: 2. Pattern Detection

blocks.content: {"headers":["Field","Detail"],"rows":[["Pattern","Composable rule simulation. Two independent divisibility checks whose results combine, not a data structure pattern like two pointers or a sliding window."],["Difficulty","Easy"],["Tags","Math, Simulation, Loops"],["Interview Focus","Composable checks over hardcoded combinations, avoiding magic numbers, and optionally replacing the modulo operator with cheap counters for less work per step."]]}

blocks.text: 3. Understand the Problem

Given a number n, print every number from 1 to n. But there is a twist for certain numbers. If a number is divisible by 3, print Fizz instead of the number. If it is divisible by 5, print Buzz instead. If it is divisible by both 3 and 5, print FizzBuzz. Every other number is printed as it is.

blocks.title: Analogy: The Stamping Conveyor Belt
blocks.text: Picture numbered boxes moving one by one on a factory conveyor belt. A stamping machine is set to stamp the word Fizz on every third box, and a second machine stamps Buzz on every fifth box. When a box happens to be both the third box and the fifth box at the same time, both machines stamp it, so it comes out reading FizzBuzz. A box that no machine touches simply keeps rolling forward with its own number visible. Solving the problem is just simulating this belt, number by number.

blocks.caption: The four rules and what each one produces

blocks.text: Example: n = 1

The smallest possible input. There is only one number, it is not divisible by 3 or 5, so the output is just the number itself: 1. Small inputs like this are worth checking separately since they often expose off by one mistakes in the loop bounds.
5. How Should We Think?
Before writing any code, it helps to reason through the problem out loud, the way an interviewer wants to see, one observation at a time.

blocks.title: How Should We Think?
blocks.text:
Observation 1: There are exactly two independent rules here, not three: divisible by 3, and divisible by 5.

Observation 2: A number can satisfy zero, one, or both rules at once. Nothing stops 15 from being divisible by 3 and by 5 at the same time.

Observation 3: A plain if/elif chain checking 3 then 5 silently drops the second rule the moment the first one matches.

Observation 4: The two rules cannot be treated as competing branches. They have to be treated as independent checks whose effects combine.

That reasoning alone, without writing a single line of code, already tells us the brute force elif chain needs its combined case checked first, and hints that a cleaner, composable version exists underneath it.
6. Brute Force Solution

The most direct way to solve this is to check every rule for every number, one after another, in a fixed order. Since a number can satisfy more than one rule (like 15 satisfying both the 3 rule and the 5 rule), the combined case has to be checked first, otherwise the code would print only Fizz or only Buzz and lose the other half of the answer.
Step by step algorithm

items: Loop through every number i from 1 to n.
If i is divisible by 15, print FizzBuzz and move to the next number.
Otherwise, if i is divisible by 3, print Fizz and move on.
Otherwise, if i is divisible by 5, print Buzz and move on.
Otherwise, print i itself.

blocks.caption: Brute force decision flow for a single number i

blocks.text: Why the code is written this way

items: The combined check (i mod 15 == 0) comes first because elif only evaluates branches until one matches, so checking 3 or 5 before 15 would let the combined case get swallowed by whichever check comes first.
The loop bound uses n + 1 in Python, or <= n in Java and C++, specifically so the number n itself is included, a classic place for an off by one slip.
Each branch stores a string rather than the raw number, so the same result list can hold a mix of transformed words and plain numbers without any type juggling later.

blocks.text: 7. Analyze the Brute Force

This solution works because the combined check (divisible by 15) is placed before the individual 3 and 5 checks. That ordering guarantees a number that satisfies both rules is never mistakenly reported as only Fizz or only Buzz.

blocks.title: Time and Space Complexity
blocks.text:
Time: O(n). The loop runs exactly n times, and each iteration does a constant number of modulo checks.
Space: O(n) for the output list itself, or O(1) extra space if the numbers are printed directly instead of stored.

Limitation: the logic only scales by hand. If a third rule were added, say multiples of 7 print Bazz, the number of combined cases to check by hand doubles for every new rule (3 rules already means up to 8 combinations). The 15 in the code is also a magic number, it works only because 15 happens to be 3 times 5, and that relationship is not obvious just by reading the code.
8. Optimize the Solution

blocks.title: The Optimization Journey
blocks.text:
Why brute force fails to scale: hardcoding every combination by hand only stays manageable while there are just two rules.

What it wastes: mental effort. Every new rule doubles the number of hand ordered combinations that must be checked correctly.

Can we avoid checking combinations at all: yes, if each rule is tested completely on its own, ignoring what the other rule decided.

Can the results combine instead of being chosen: yes, by building the answer as a string and letting each rule append its own piece to it.

The composable idea: start empty, let the 3 rule add Fizz, let the 5 rule add Buzz, and treat an empty result as the signal to fall back to the plain number.

The brute force approach hardcodes every combination of rules by hand. The optimization is to stop thinking in combinations and instead treat each rule as independent and composable: check divisibility by 3 on its own, check divisibility by 5 on its own, and let both checks contribute to the same answer.

The intuition is to build the answer as a string, starting empty, and let each rule append its own word if it applies. A number divisible by both 3 and 5 naturally ends up with both words appended in order, without ever needing a hardcoded 15 check. A number divisible by neither is left with an empty string, which is the signal to fall back to the plain number.
9. Optimized Solution

For every number, start with an empty string. Check divisibility by 3 on its own and append Fizz if it matches. Then check divisibility by 5 on its own and append Buzz if it matches. If nothing was appended, the string is still empty, so use the number itself.
Dry run for i = 15

blocks.content: {"headers":["Step","Check","s after this step","Why"],"rows":[["1","Start with s = empty","(empty)","Every number starts with a clean slate before either rule is checked."],["2","i mod 3 == 0, so append Fizz","Fizz","The 3 rule is checked completely on its own, independent of the 5 rule."],["3","i mod 5 == 0, so append Buzz","FizzBuzz","The 5 rule is also checked on its own; since it also matches, its word is appended right after Fizz."],["4","s is not empty, print s","FizzBuzz (final output)","Because s already has content, the fallback to the plain number never triggers."]]}

blocks.caption: Optimized string building flow for a single number i

blocks.text: Why This Works

Every number falls into exactly one of four cases: divisible by neither, by 3 only, by 5 only, or by both. Because the two checks are independent if statements rather than an if/elif chain, a number divisible by both 3 and 5 triggers both appends in order, automatically producing FizzBuzz without ever hardcoding that combination. A number divisible by neither triggers neither append, leaving the string empty, which is exactly the signal used to fall back to the plain number. Order is preserved for free, since the loop still walks from 1 to n in order and appends each result to the end of the same list.

blocks.content: {"headers":["Case","What Happens","Result"],"rows":[["Divisible by neither","Neither if statement runs, s stays empty","Falls back to the number itself"],["Divisible by 3 only","First if runs, appends Fizz","Fizz"],["Divisible by 5 only","Second if runs, appends Buzz","Buzz"],["Divisible by both","Both if statements run, in order","FizzBuzz"]]}

blocks.text: Code walkthrough

items: Both divisibility checks are plain if statements, not if/elif, specifically so a number satisfying both conditions runs both appends instead of stopping after the first one.

The empty string fallback (s or str(i) in Python, the ternary check in Java and C++) has to come after both appends, never before, or it would treat a number that has not yet checked the 5 rule as already finished.
Starting s empty inside the loop, not outside it, is what prevents one number's Fizz or Buzz from leaking into the next number's result.

blocks.title: Time and Space Complexity
blocks.text:
Time: O(n), one pass over the numbers with constant work per number.
Space: O(1) extra space per number, since the string built for each number has a small bounded length regardless of how large n is.
10. Further Optimization (If Possible)

Both solutions above use the modulo operator to test divisibility. Modulo is a division under the hood, and division is one of the more expensive basic operations for a processor compared to addition or comparison. In a performance sensitive setting, that cost can be avoided entirely.

Intuition: instead of asking "is i divisible by 3", keep a counter that simply counts up from the last time Fizz was printed. When that counter reaches 3, it means exactly 3 steps have passed, so this is a multiple of 3, print Fizz and reset the counter to 0. The same idea applies to a second counter for Buzz with a target of 5. This replaces every modulo check with a cheap increment and comparison.

What changed: two counters, fizz and buzz, both starting at 0. On every step both counters increase by 1. When fizz reaches 3, append Fizz and reset fizz to 0. When buzz reaches 5, append Buzz and reset buzz to 0.
Dry run for i = 13 to 15

blocks.content: {"headers":["i","fizz","buzz","Output","Why"],"rows":[["13","1","3","13","Neither counter has reached its target yet, so nothing is appended."],["14","2","4","14","Still short of both targets, still nothing appended."],["15","3, so append Fizz and reset to 0","5, so append Buzz and reset to 0","FizzBuzz","Both counters happen to hit their targets on the exact same step, appending both words and resetting both counters back to 0."]]}

blocks.caption: Counter based flow that replaces modulo with increments

blocks.text: Code walkthrough

items: Both counters increment unconditionally on every single iteration, before any comparison, because every number is one step closer to the next multiple of 3 and the next multiple of 5 regardless of what happens this round.

A counter resets to 0 only inside its own if block, immediately after firing, which is what keeps it counting steps since the last multiple instead of drifting away from the true divisibility pattern.
Using == 3 and == 5 instead of >= 3 and >= 5 is intentional: an exact equality check paired with an immediate reset guarantees a counter can never overshoot its target.

blocks.text: Why multiples of 15 are the special case

blocks.caption: The Fizz cycle and Buzz cycle only reset together at their lowest common multiple

blocks.text: The reason 15 is the number where both rules fire together is not a coincidence written into the problem, it falls directly out of basic arithmetic: 15 is the lowest common multiple of 3 and 5. The Fizz counter completes a full cycle of length 3 five times over, and the Buzz counter completes a full cycle of length 5 three times over, and the very first point where both cycles reset to 0 at the same moment is step 15. That is exactly why the classic elif chain has to special case i mod 15 == 0, and exactly why the composable and counter based versions never need to special case it at all, the alignment happens automatically.

blocks.title: Time and Space Complexity
blocks.text:
Time: O(n), still one pass over the numbers, the same as before.
Space: O(1) extra space, just two integer counters regardless of n.

blocks.text: 12. Key Takeaways

The core pattern here is composable divisibility checks: instead of hardcoding every combination of rules, test each rule independently and let the results combine naturally. This same pattern extends cleanly to any number of extra rules without the combinations exploding.
Common Mistakes

items: Checking i mod 3 or i mod 5 in an elif chain before checking the combined case: because elif stops at the first match, a multiple of 15 gets reported as only Fizz (or only Buzz), silently losing half the correct answer.

Off by one in the loop bounds, such as looping while i < n instead of i <= n: this quietly drops the number n itself from the output, a mistake easy to miss since n is usually not divisible by 3 or 5.

Forgetting to convert the number to a string before concatenating it with Fizz or Buzz text in a statically typed language: this either fails to compile or silently produces the wrong result, depending on the language.

Letting a counter drift past its target, such as using >= instead of == when checking the fizz or buzz counter: without an exact equality check and an immediate reset, the counter can overshoot and desynchronize from the true multiples for the rest of the loop.

blocks.text: Interview Tips

FizzBuzz is often used as a quick warm up question, so interviewers pay close attention to how clean the logic is, not just whether it works. Writing the composable version instead of the hardcoded elif chain, and being ready for the natural follow up question ("what if we add multiples of 7?"), signals stronger fundamentals than a working but rigid brute force answer.

blocks.title: If The Interviewer Says This, Think This
blocks.text:
If the interviewer says "can you avoid the modulo operator", think: switch to the two counter approach.
If the interviewer says "what if we add another rule", think: composable independent checks, never another elif branch.
If the interviewer says "keep this O(1) extra space", think: print each result directly inside the loop instead of building and returning a full list.
Interview Follow-up Questions

items: Can you solve this without the modulo operator at all?
What if a third rule were added, for example printing Bazz for multiples of 7?
Can you produce the output one string at a time, lazily, instead of building the whole list upfront, for a very large n?
How would the solution change if the two words themselves, Fizz and Buzz, were passed in as parameters instead of being fixed?
Can you write this with no if/else at all, using a generic list of divisor and word rules and a loop over that list?

blocks.text: Pattern Connections

items: Any problem with several independent conditions that can overlap on the same input, where the results need to combine rather than the first match winning.
Bitmasking problems, where each bit represents one independent condition and the final result naturally combines every bit that is set, the same way Fizz and Buzz combine here.
Rule engines in real systems, such as a pricing or discount system where multiple independent promotions can apply to the same order at once and their effects need to stack.

The counter instead of modulo trick reappears anywhere a loop needs to detect every kth iteration cheaply, such as flushing a buffer or logging progress every 100th record without dividing on every single iteration.

blocks.title: Complexity Summary
blocks.text: All three approaches run in O(n) time. The brute force and optimized versions use O(1) extra space per step, and the counter based version is the cheapest per step since it avoids the modulo operator entirely, which matters most when n is very large.
13. Final Summary

items: Pattern: composable divisibility simulation, independent checks whose results combine instead of compete.

Core Idea: test each rule (divisible by 3, divisible by 5) completely on its own, so a number satisfying both rules naturally ends up with both effects, instead of hardcoding every combination by hand.
Time: O(n) across every version shown here.
Space: O(1) extra per step (excluding the output list itself); the counter based version also avoids the modulo operator entirely.

Most Important Observation: the FizzBuzz case is not really a third rule, it is just what happens when the two true, independent rules overlap, and 15 is special only because it is the lowest common multiple of 3 and 5.
Interview Difficulty: easy on the surface, but the composability and modulo avoiding follow ups quickly separate a strong answer from a rigid one.
One line memory trick: do not ask which rule wins, ask which rules apply, and let them stack.
